svg.title: Saltzer and Schroeder's eight design principles
svg.desc: Eight cards, one per principle from the 1975 paper: economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism, and psychological acceptability. Each card states the principle and what it is protecting against. A footer records that the same paper adds work factor and compromise recording from physical security and notes they apply only imperfectly to computer systems, and that defense in depth and separation of duties are commonly cited alongside these but are not part of the eight.
svg.text: Saltzer and Schroeder's eight design principles
Design heuristics from the 1975 paper, not requirements of any standard. They constrain each other, so applying one can weaken another.
1. Economy of mechanism
Keep the protection design as simple and small as it can be.
Against: complexity that hides flaws no review will find.
2. Fail-safe defaults
Base access on permission rather than exclusion: deny unless granted.
Against: a mistake in the rules opening access instead of closing it.
3. Complete mediation
Check every access to every object on every invocation.
Against: a stale or indefinitely cached decision outliving the right.
4. Open design
Security rests on protected secrets, not on a secret design.
Against: collapse the day the architecture or source becomes known.
5. Separation of privilege
Require more than one key or condition to release a critical action.
Against: one compromised credential completing the whole operation.
6. Least privilege
Every subject runs with the minimum privileges its task needs.
Against: lateral movement and escalation after an account is taken.
7. Least common mechanism
Minimize mechanism shared between users and trust domains.
Against: leakage through a shared cache, kernel, or library.
8. Psychological acceptability
A mechanism people find intrusive is a mechanism people route around.
Against: shadow workflows that silently remove the control.
The same paper adds two more principles taken from physical security — work factor and compromise recording — and states that they apply only
imperfectly to computer systems, because the cost of defeating a mechanism is often not calculable.
Defense in depth and separation of duties are widely cited alongside these, but they are not part of the original eight.
